head: working-tree
subject: QUIC PADDING skip scans sixteen bytes per iteration
change: parseFrameWithAllocator, parseFrameInto and the Initial-flight CRYPTO reassembler now skip PADDING runs with one shared scanner instead of std.mem.findNonePos, which is a scalar nested loop over each byte. The helper compares 32-byte vectors against zero, uses std.simd.firstTrue to locate the first non-zero lane, and finishes the tail with u128, u64 and byte loops. The first-non-zero result and consumed length are unchanged, including a payload that is entirely PADDING.
notes: The benchmark payload is 1200 zero bytes; padding-only measures a full PADDING run and padding-before-PING appends a PING frame. The 32-byte vector comparison uses std.simd.firstTrue, so the lane index is endian-independent; the u128/u64/byte tails preserve the same first-non-zero semantics for short payloads and partial words. The QUIC suite covers overlong and fully padded payloads, and the full library suite passes with the change. The Initial-flight CRYPTO reassembler calls the same public helper, so long datagram padding is skipped with identical semantics there as well. The quic-go HTTP/3 interop matrix was re-run after the vector change and passes 9/9, exercising padded Initial packets in both endpoint roles.

interop.note: QUIC v1/v2 peer, cancel, redirect, pool and informational matrix against quic-go. Initial packets are padded to 1200 bytes, so the vector PADDING skip is exercised in real handshakes in both client and server roles.
